## Overview
If you’re hunting for the **best budget gaming PC build 2026**, you’re in the right spot. This guide walks you through a balanced parts list that hits sweet‑spot performance without breaking the bank. We focus on current‑gen components that offer strong frame rates at 1080p and decent 1440p play, all while keeping upgrade paths open for the next few years. Let’s dive into each piece and see how they fit together.

## CPU Choice
For a budget build in 2026, AMD’s Ryzen 5 7600X remains a stellar pick. Six cores and twelve threads, paired with Zen 4 architecture, give you solid multi‑tasking and gaming performance. It pairs nicely with affordable B650 motherboards and supports DDR5 memory, which is now mainstream. If you prefer Intel, the Core i5‑13400F offers similar gaming prowess at a slightly lower price, though it lacks PCIe 5.0 support. Either way, aim for a CPU that stays under $180 to keep the total build cost in check.

## GPU Pick
The graphics card is where most of your gaming budget goes. In 2026, the AMD Radeon RX 7700 XT hits the sweet spot for 1080p ultra and 1440p high settings, usually landing around $260–$280. NVIDIA’s RTX 4060 Ti 8 GB is a close competitor, offering DLSS 3 and ray‑tracing perks at a similar price. Choose the card that best matches your preferred brand ecosystem and the games you play most. Both options provide enough VRAM for upcoming titles without forcing you into the premium tier.

## Motherboard & RAM
A B650 chipset motherboard pairs perfectly with the Ryzen 5 7600X, offering PCIe 5.0 slots for future GPUs and ample USB‑C connectivity. Look for models with solid VRMs and at least two M.2 slots; prices hover between $110–$130. For memory, 16 GB (2×8 GB) of DDR5‑5600 is the baseline. If you can stretch to 32 GB, you’ll future‑proof for heavier multitasking or content creation, but 16 GB remains more than enough for pure gaming.

## Storage Options
Speed matters, so an NVMe SSD is a must. A 1 TB PCIe 4.0 drive like the WD Black SN850X provides fast load times and plenty of room for your library, usually under $80. If you need extra space for media, add a cheap 2 TB SATA SSD or a 4 TB HDD—both are inexpensive and easy to install later. Keeping your OS and games on the NVMe ensures snappy performance.

## PSU & Case
Reliability starts with the power supply. A 650 W 80+ Gold unit from Corsair, Seasonic, or EVGA gives you headroom for upgrades and stable power delivery. Expect to spend $80–$100. For the case, choose a mid‑tower with good airflow, tool‑free drive bays, and cable‑management features. Models like the NZXT H510 or Cooler Master MasterBox Q300L sit around $70–$90 and look clean while keeping temps low.
